summary.value: This paper studies FedExProx, an existing proximal-point method for federated optimization, with inexact local solvers. The analysis of the method is provided under the assumptions of: 1) individual convexity and smoothness, 2) global strong convexity, and 3) Interpolation. Finally, the number of local gradient oracle calls required to achieve the established communication complexity is provided for GD and AGD.

strengths.value:
1. The motivation of the paper is clear. The first paper that analyzes FedExProx assumes exact subproblem solvers, which cannot be implemented. 
2. The theory is backed by reasonable proofs.

weaknesses.value:
The contribution is overall a bit limited. 

> Scope 

The main contribution of the paper is to extend the analysis of FedExProx to allow inexact local solutions in the proximal steps. This has already been partially done in [1] (Appendix E) using the definition of Absolute approximation, under PL conditions.

FedExProx was originally proposed and analyzed in [1,2]. These papers also study client sampling, adaptive stepsize, and demonstrate the benefits of extrapolation in terms of communication speed-up under interpolation.

In contrast, the current submission focuses only on the strong-convexity-with-interpolation setting (full participation and constant stepsize), which is a bit more restrictive. (Note that the current theory breaks when $\mu \to 0$.) Moreover, the proof strategy for the outer iterations (communication) follows [1] almost directly, relying on the (S)GD reformulation and Moreau envelope. The main difference is the addition of an error term due to the inexact proximal-point step. 

> Novelty and results. 

FedExProx can be reformulated as a standard GD iteration (eqns (10)–(11)), with the only change being that the gradient is now biased. The bias term appears in eqn (11), and the analysis follows that of [1, 2] by additionally bounding this bias under the stated assumptions. These error terms then accumulate and appear in the final convergence rate. In this sense, the novelty is limited to handling an additional and simple bias term.

Furthermore, the analysis of GD (or SGD) with biased gradients — and its connection to compression — is well-established in the literature [3]. More connections and better theory can be done under approximately smooth assumptions [4], which is not considered here.
 
>  Comparisons with other methods

Given that this work targets federated optimization, the comparisons with other FL methods are a bit limited, both in theory and in experiments. Several state-of-the-art federated proximal-point methods can achieve stronger convergence guarantees (including acceleration), better local computation complexity, under weaker assumptions. The discussions about other federated proximal-point methods, except FedProx, seem to be missing.





[1] The Power of Extrapolation in Federated Learning, Neurips 2024.

[2] Tighter Performance Theory of FedExProx, arxiv 2024. 

[3] On the Convergence of SGD with Biased Gradients, ICML workshop 2020.

[4] First-order methods of smooth convex optimization with inexact oracle, Mathematical Programming 2013

questions.value: 1. It would be great to validate the theory by comparing AGD against GD as different local solvers in numerical experiments.

summary.value:
This paper revisits FedExProx and removes a key unrealistic assumption from prior theory: that clients compute the proximal operator exactly. The authors provide convergence guarantees in the smooth, globally strongly convex regime under inexact proximal solves, showing convergence to a neighborhood under absolute error and exact convergence under a relative/inexactness control. They further connect the inexactness term to biased compression / biased-gradient analysis and study local iteration complexity for achieving required inexactness levels.
This paper is technically correct and well-motivated, and clearly written, but major concern from the reviewers is whether it constitutes a sufficiently broad or novel theoretical contribution.

reviewer_concerns.value: the concerns are: 1) limited/incremental novelty; 2) restrictive assumptions, I guess this one is OK; 3) the empirical validation is seen as illustrative, not decisive; this one I agree, and it is important

reviewer_scores.value: The rebuttal is helpful, but may not change the reviewers' score

comment.value:
Thank you for your timely response. 

We respectfully disagree with the implication that a contribution is only "novel" if it introduces an entirely new analytical tool. In optimization research, theoretical advances are almost always achieved by extending, reconfiguring, or repurposing existing frameworks, such as biased gradient models, compression operators, stability arguments, etc. The value of a contribution lies in whether these components are combined in a way that yields new insights or new guarantees that were previously unknown, not in whether every piece of the machinery is new in isolation.

Regarding assumption 2.7, we have stated that Theorem 3.2 and Theorem 4.2 are simplified versions of Theorem F.1 and Theorem F.5 in the appendix, which are obtained without interpolation (or shared minimizer) assumption. The result will include an additional controllable neighborhood term due to the difference in the personalized federated learning solution and the true solution. So the assumption is not needed.

As we have stated, our reformulation and its link to biased compression already allow one to obtain analogous results in the general convex setting, and we also provide empirical evidence in general deep learning problems that our methods does work, even without assumptions such as smoothness and convexity.

summary.value: The paper presents an improved convergence analysis of the FedExProx algorithm by removing the assumption that the proximal operator is exactly computed. FedExProx is a recently proposed extension of the FedProx algorithm that combines the proximal local updates of FedProx with the global stepsize schedule proposed in FedExp.

strengths.value: - The paper fills a gap in the analysis of the previous work that introduced FedExProx by removing the assumption of exactness of the local proximal operator.

weaknesses.value:
- While the paper's analysis is sound and well-presented, its contribution is narrowly focused on a single variant of FedAvg—the FedExProx algorithm. It is unclear how the insights from the analysis apply more broadly and how they guide the design of federated optimization algorithms in general.
- In the literature review, please cite previous analyses of FedProx, such as FedNova (https://arxiv.org/abs/2007.07481), which includes as a special case the convergence analysis of FedProx (with $\tau$ local updates at each client, and thus inexact solution of the proximal operator). I also have questions (see below) about how the analysis of this work relates to that analysis of FedProx.
- The FedExProx algorithm considers an extrapolation parameter $\alpha_k$ that varies with the round number $k$. However, Theorem 3.2 and Theorem 4.2 assume that $\alpha_k = \alpha$, fixed across rounds. Wouldn't this reduce the algorithm being analyzed to FedProx?
- The simulation result plots are not easily readable. Please increase the font size.

questions.value: - In practice, clients are likely to simply perform $\tau$ local SGD updates where gradients are computed for the local objective plus the proximal penalty term. I don't quite understand how one would find the inexactness $\epsilon_1$ of the local solution. In the case of local FedProx-style SGD updates, the convergence analysis in https://arxiv.org/abs/2007.07481 can be applied. How does the analysis in this paper (and FedExProx) relate to the prior work? Would you need to consider an $\epsilon_1$ that decays with the number of communication rounds completed?

comment.value: I greatly  appreciate your response to my feedback. Given the explanations on the experimental study and the work’s theoretical nature, my initial concerns in this regard have been sufficiently clarified. However, I remain unsatisfied with the explanations on my core concerns around novelty of analysis and validity of assumption. Regarding the claimed "new proof technique", framing the analysis around biased SGD and compression theory does not inherently constitute a novel theoretical contribution, as these are established tools in optimization. As for assumptions, the Assumption 2.7 corresponds exactly to the so-called *interpolation regime* assumed in the original FedExProx paper (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2405.13766, Assumption 2). For the strongly convex setting considered herein, this assumption essentially implies that all clients share a common unique global minimizer $x_\star$. Moreover, dismissing smoothness as "standard" overlooks its mismatch with real-world non-smooth FL scenarios, and the reliance on global strong convexity (even for linear rate results) severely restricts practical relevance.

Thank you for taking time to review our paper, below, we provide a response addressing each of your concern.

> Weakness 1: It is unclear how the insights from the analysis apply more broadly and how they guide the design of federated optimization algorithms in general.

Thank you for this observation. While our study highlights FedExProx, the theoretical contribution is not specific to this algorithm. The extrapolation mechanism introduces a non-trivial interaction between: (i) the inexactness of local proximal updates and (ii) the contraction properties induced by server-side extrapolation, which is a phenomenon that, to our knowledge, has not been analyzed in the federated optimization literature.

More importantly, the main insight of our work concerns a structural property of proximal type methods under inexact local computation in distributed settings. When proximal subproblems are solved locally and aggregated at the server, the widely used choice of a server stepsize of $1$ is generally not optimal. Our analysis reveals the underlying mechanism, which is that the inexact local proximal mappings introduce a persistent bias term in the global fixed-point recursion, and extrapolation increases the contraction strength of that recursion, thereby reducing the impact of inexactness and improving the global convergence rate.

This mechanism is not limited to FedProx/FedExProx, our results position extrapolation as a principled acceleration technique that is orthogonal to other standard strategies in FL. Extrapolation operates at the server level, modifying the global fixed-point structure in a way that complements, rather than replaces, other forms of acceleration. 

> Weakness 2: In the literature review, please ...

Thanks for pointing this out, we have improved the literature review section to include more related work and explanantions for better clarity. This will be reflected in the next version of the paper.

> Weakness 3: The FedExProx algorithm considers an extrapolation parameter $\alpha_k$ that varies with the round number $k$, ... Wouldn't this reduce the algorithm being analyzed to FedProx?

We would like to clarify that the standard FedProx analysis does not contain any notion of a server stepsize, nor does it provide theory supporting the choice $\alpha_k \equiv 1$. In our framework, FedProx is recovered only as the special case $\alpha_k \equiv 1$.
Our analysis is the first to show that this choice is generally not optimal when local proximal solves are inexact. We analyze the constant case first because it cleanly exposes the contraction mechanism under inexact local solves. We also justify adaptive stepsize choices, the theory cleanly accommodates variable $\alpha_k$.

> Weakness 4: The simulation result plots are not easily readable. Please increase the font size.

We have increased the font size as per requested.

> Questions: How one would find the inexactness of the solution. 

We thank the reviewer for this thoughtful question. In our work, $\varepsilon$ stands for theoretical accuracy levels but not quantities the algorithm needs to measure. In practice are not computed exactly. The FedNova analysis cited by the reviewer fits directly into this framework.
As for decay, a fixed $\varepsilon_1$ yields convergence to a neighborhood, as in prior work. If one desires higher precision, it can be made to decay for better precision as the reviewer has pointed out. But this is not required, using relative inexactness removes the neighborhood entirely, and our theory shows that the acceleration from extrapolation remains effective without needing any decay of the local error.

summary.value: This paper presents an inexact analysis on the convergence of the FedExProx (FedProx with extrapolation, Li et al., 2024a) algoithm under practical inexact updates. For smooth and strongly convex problems, it shows that inexact updates lead to convergence to a solution neighborhood, and relative approximation eliminates bias for exact convergence. The authors further refined their analysis by linking proximal inexactness to biased compression theory, validating the robustness of extrapolation even with imperfect client computations. The theoretical findings are complemented with a set of empirical evidence on federated quadratic optimization and CNN training tasks for validation.

strengths.value:
1. The paper addresses a practical gap of FedExProx by relaxing the unrealistic exact proximal operator assumption, establishing convergence under inexact updates, which bridges theory and practical FL applications.

2. The paper is generally well organized and clearly presented, with sufficient technical details and proactive supplementary analyses offered to enhance readability and applicability.

3. The idea of linking proximal inexactness to biased compression is somewhat interesting, and it turns out to be useful for showing the robustness of extrapolation to inexact proximal operator evaluations.

weaknesses.value:
The major concern goes to the novely of analysis and significance of results, given that this work essentially represents a theoretical contribution to FL. 

1. The convergence analysis is incrementally novel, mostly extending existing proof techniques without any particularly new ideas/tools developed. While the core results are intuitive and interesting, they are not expected to generate significant impact on FL research, both in thoery and practice. 

2. The analysis relies on overly strong assumptions, such as smoothness, global strong convexity, and shared client solutions, which rarely hold in real-world settings (e.g., non-convex, non-smooth deep federated learning). These assumptions, especially when combined, greatly limit the generalizability of the results.

3. The provided experimental study is illustrative but rather weak, in the sense that it fails to align with real scenarios and theoretical scope. Concerning the experiment on quadratic programming (in the main text), only synthetic data is used without comparisons to closely relevant baseline methods like FedAvg (which also inexactly minimizes local objectives with multiple iterations of SGD). Concerning the DL experiments on ResNet training (in the appendix), there exists a clear disconnect between theory and experiment as the key assumptions like smoothness/strong convexity are not fulfilled by the considered DL models. Such a gap weakens the convincingness of this group of experimental results, though they were observed in a more realistic setting.

questions.value: Is there any way to analyze the (inexact) FedExProx method in non-convex (or non-smooth) settings that are commonly considered in FL studies?

comment.value:
Thank you for taking time to review our paper, below, we provide a response addressing each of your concern.

> Weakness 1: Scope

We would like to clarify several points regarding the relation to [1] and [2] and the scope of our analysis.

```Relation to [2]```:

The notion of FedExProx and the extrapolation framework were introduced in our earlier work [2]. Appendix E of [1] contains only a premature and partial variant of the idea, restricted to absolute approximations under PL conditions and without any theoretical justification of the effectiveness of extrapolation under inexactness. In contrast, the present submission provides the first complete and rigorous analysis showing why extrapolation remains effective when the local proximal solves are inexact, and how it strengthens the global contraction.


```Strong convexity```:
Global strong convexity is a standard assumption in FL analysis and is widely used to study proximal methods. Our results in this regime give linear convergence in squared distance, which is exactly the expected guarantee. Taking $\mu \rightarrow 0$ is not meaningful in this context because the guarantee itself changes: in the convex case one naturally obtains function-value suboptimality bounds instead, and the same framework can be extended to that setting, which is why the theoretical insights matter.
Importantly, our empirical results already show that the method behaves well in both convex and non-convex problems, underscoring that the theory captures the essential mechanism even beyond the strongly convex regime. 


```Interpolation assumptions ...```:
Our analysis simply does not rely on interpolation condition. 


```Adaptive stepsizes and partial participation```:
Although the main text emphasizes constant stepsize for clarity, we do provide results for adaptive stepsizes and partial participation in the appendix. 

```Proof technique```:
Our proof strategy is substantially different from [1]. While [1] relies on a clean SGD reformulation and the Moreau envelope under exact solves, our analysis must handle a biased fixed-point recursion induced by inexact proximal evaluations. This leads to a structure analogous to biased SGD, which requires very different tools and yields qualitatively new insights about error propagation and extrapolation, compared to the standard analysis of SGD.

In summary, the contribution of this paper is neither a minor extension nor a restatement of [1]. It provides a new theoretical mechanism for understanding extrapolation under inexact proximal steps, covers settings beyond interpolation, and includes adaptive stepsize and partial-participation results.

> Novelty and results

```Relation to [1] and [2].```:
We respectfully disagree with the assertion that our contribution is a simple extension of [1,2]. Our analysis does not follow [1] which requires interpolation that we do not. And the extrapolated proximal framework was first introduced in our earlier work, and the analysis in [2] corresponds only to an exact and restricted subcase of the method we proposed under a different assumption. The present submission develops the full theory for inexact proximal steps under extrapolation, a setting that [1,2] do not treat and for which their arguments do not apply.

```Extra bias term.```:
The additional term is not a trivial extension. Just as biased SGD cannot be analyzed by simply reusing the proofs for SGD, the introduction of inexactness fundamentally changes the recursion. The analysis no longer follows from the exact case in [1], and the substantially different proof strategy in our paper is itself evidence of this.

```On the connection to biased SGD and compression.```:
We are claiming that the inexact proximal updates with extrapolation are connected to both biased SGD and biased compression, not the later two are connected, which is well known.


> Comparisons with other methods:

Our work here is to justify extrapolation acts as a orthogonal acceleration technique to existing proximal algorithms, which can be added on top of the existing SOTA. Our theory rigorously explains why the server stepsize $1$ is not inherently optimal and why extrapolation remains effective even when the local proximal updates are inexact. This provides a principled foundation for incorporating extrapolation on top of existing proximal frameworks.

> Question:
Thanks for the suggestion. We have already done that in our deep learning experiments, and we are updating our plots in the numerical experiments as well. This will be reflected in the next version of the paper.

Thank you for taking time to review our paper, below, we provide a response addressing each of your concern.

> Weakness 1: The convergence analysis is incrementally novel, mostly extending existing proof techniques without any particularly new ideas/tools developed ...

The proof technique we develop is new and does not follow directly from prior analyses. Our approach relies on a reformulation grounded in biased SGD and compression theory, a perspective not used or mentioned in the original FedExProx paper. Furthermore, we eliminate the interpolation assumption, resulting in conditions that are significantly less restrictive than those used in earlier extrapolation-based analyses of FedProx. The key contribution of our work is a rigorous demonstration that inexactness does not diminish the effectiveness of extrapolation, a finding that is further supported by our deep learning experiments on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 (instead of CNN mentioned by the reviewer).

> Weakness 2: The analysis relies on overly strong assumptions, such as smoothness, global strong convexity, and shared client solutions, which rarely hold in real-world settings (e.g., non-convex, non-smooth deep federated learning). These assumptions, especially when combined, greatly limit the generalizability of the results.

Our analysis does not rely on any form of shared client solutions. The smoothness assumption is standard in federated optimization and is widely used across the literature, including in large-scale training settings such as LLMs. Global strong convexity is assumed only to obtain a linear rate in squared distance, while in the general convex case one can derive the corresponding sublinear convergence guarantees using the same reformulation approach.

> Weakness 3:

Our synthetic experiments validate the theory in a fully controlled setting where all assumptions are satisfied. The deep learning experiments then demonstrate that the same insights continue to hold in a more realistic, non-convex regime. Together, they confirm that there is no inconsistency between theory and experiment: the synthetic results illustrate the precise mechanisms proved in the analysis, while the deep learning results show that these mechanisms remain effective in practical, non-convex settings.


> Questions:

Yes. Our experiments already demonstrate that the acceleration mechanism persists in non-convex and non-smooth settings, which strongly suggests that the method is not restricted to the strongly convex regime. A theoretical treatment in these settings is also entirely feasible: by adopting standard assumptions such as weak convexity, prox-regularity, or other common non-convex conditions used in FL analysis, one can extend our arguments in a similar manner. This is precisely the value of our contribution: we provide a general analytical framework for handling extrapolated proximal updates with inexactness, which can be adapted beyond the strongly convex case.
